newsitem.title: FRANCE: French economy needs shock treatment - Socialists.
newsitem.headline: French economy needs shock treatment - Socialists.

text.p: France's economy needs shock treatment to boost sluggish growth, cut unemployment and combat inequality, Socialist leader Lionel Jospin said on Tuesday.
Outlining his party's economic programme for a March 1998 general election, Jospin said the Socialists would provide the required jolt if they won.

"We need to create a shock with a new policy of growth, which is why I believe in the need for an original policy that strongly attacks unemployment and inequality, and seizes France's problems while building a Europe that is both ambitious and attainable," Jospin told a news conference.
Conservative Prime Minister Alain Juppe retorted in parliament that the Socialist platform would "lead France back into the spiral of decline".

France is suffering from record 12.7 percent unemployment and slow growth, and the population is deeply sceptical of prospects for a lasting economic rebound. The pressure to lower deficits to qualify for a single European currency is an extra constraint that would not relent under a different government.
To counter the problems, Jospin offered a plan to reduce the work week to 35 hours without cutting pay, create 700,000 jobs -- mostly for the young -- and reform health insurance payments.
He said his policies offered a clear alternative to those of the centre-right government, which he accused of focusing on electoral inducements at the expense of fundamental reform.
He contrasted his detailed policy statement with what he called the woolly "communications events" staged recently by President Jacques Chirac and Juppe.
But his proposals, while more reliant on state action, were strikingly similar to some government policies in the last 18 months.
If they won the election, which opinion polls suggest is unlikely, the Socialists' hands would be tied by many of the same constraints hobbling Juppe's government.
Though the ruling coalition still leads in most polls, the Socialists and their left-wing allies have edged to within striking distance.

A February 18 poll by BVA for weekly Paris Match found that the left would win 31.5 percent of the vote, an increase of two percentage points from a month earlier, compared to 36.5 percent for the majority, a decline of less than one point.

Juppe's government has removed some of the burden of funding the welfare state from payroll charges, launched youth employment initiatives and enabled companies to reduce the work week, all without making a dent in the jobless rate.
Jospin charged that Chirac was locked into backward-looking policies that kept the economy from achieving its growth potential, which he put at three percent a year.
In 1996, the economy grew 1.3 percent and the government has said it expects growth of at least 2.3 percent this year.
"A new situation demands new policies. Our problem is no longer inflation, which has been beaten, nor our trade balance, which is in surplus. Our problem is mass unemployment," he said.

While saying the primary solution to France's jobs crisis lay in stronger private sector growth, Jospin pledged to create 350,000 public sector jobs in two years by creating a new long-term work contract.
He said this five-year contract would gradually replace existing shorter-term youth employment schemes. It would be paid for by shifting money from existing initiatives.
As for the 350,000 private sector jobs he envisioned, Jospin said he would rely on a "moral obligation" among employers.
Many of these jobs could be freed up by offering retirement to employees with 40 years' service, he said. This measure would cost about eight billion francs a year for five years.
